title: MATH GAOKAO - 70
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a cubic function has an inverse on its natural domain.
questions.question: Does \(f(x)=x^3+1\) have an inverse function on \(\mathbb{R}\)?

options.label: B
options.text: No, because it is not one-to-one.

questions.explanation: The function \(f(x)=x^3+1\) is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb{R}\), since \(x^3\) is strictly increasing. Therefore, it passes the horizontal line test and is one-to-one. A one-to-one function has an inverse. Thus option A is correct.
questions.hint: Check whether the function is strictly increasing or decreasing on its entire domain.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a quadratic function has an inverse on its natural domain.
questions.question: Does \(f(x)=x^2\) have an inverse function on \(\mathbb{R}\)?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because every real number has a square.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because it is not one-to-one.

questions.explanation:
The function \(f(x)=x^2\) is not one-to-one on \(\mathbb{R}\). For example,
\[
f(2)=4 \quad \text{and} \quad f(-2)=4.
\]
Since two different inputs give the same output, the function fails the horizontal line test and has no inverse on \(\mathbb{R}\). Thus option B is correct.
questions.hint: Look for two different input values that produce the same output.

questions.concept: Existence of an Inverse Function on a Restricted Domain
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a quadratic function has an inverse on a restricted domain.
questions.question: Does \(f(x)=x^2\) have an inverse function on the restricted domain \([0,\infty)\)?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because it is one-to-one on \([0,\infty)\).

options.label: B
options.text: No, because it is still not one-to-one on \([0,\infty)\).

questions.explanation: On the restricted domain \([0,\infty)\), the function \(f(x)=x^2\) is strictly increasing. Therefore, it is one-to-one: if \(x_1\ne x_2\) and both are non-negative, then \(x_1^2\ne x_2^2\). Hence it has an inverse on this domain. Thus option A is correct.
questions.hint: Check whether the function is strictly increasing or decreasing on the restricted interval.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether an absolute value function has an inverse on its natural domain.
questions.question: Does \(f(x)=|x|\) have an inverse function on \(\mathbb{R}\)?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because absolute value is always non-negative.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because it is not one-to-one.

questions.explanation:
The function \(f(x)=|x|\) is not one-to-one on \(\mathbb{R}\). For example,
\[
f(1)=1 \quad \text{and} \quad f(-1)=1.
\]
Different inputs give the same output, so the function fails the horizontal line test and has no inverse on \(\mathbb{R}\). Thus option B is correct.
questions.hint: Find two different inputs that give the same absolute value.

questions.concept: Existence of an Inverse Function on a Restricted Domain
questions.learningObjective: Determine an interval on which a quadratic function is one-to-one and therefore has an inverse.
questions.question: For which domain restriction does \(f(x)=x^2-4x+3\) have an inverse?
questions.explanation:
Complete the square:
\[
f(x)=x^2-4x+3=(x-2)^2-1.
\]
The graph is a parabola with vertex at \(x=2\). On \((-\infty,2]\), the function is strictly decreasing, so it is one-to-one and has an inverse. On \([1,3]\), however, the function is not one-to-one; for example,
\[
f(1)=0 \quad \text{and} \quad f(3)=0.
\]
Thus option B is correct.
questions.hint: Find the vertex of the parabola, then choose an interval on which the function is strictly monotonic.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a reciprocal function has an inverse.
questions.question: Does \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x}\) have an inverse function on its natural domain \(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\)?

options.label: A
options.text: No, because it is not defined at \(x=0\).

questions.explanation:
On \(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\), the function \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x}\) is one-to-one. If \(\frac{1}{a}=\frac{1}{b}\), then \(a=b\). Therefore, it has an inverse. In fact,
\[
f(f(x))=\frac{1}{1/x}=x,
\]
so the function is its own inverse:
\[
f^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{x}.
\]
Thus option B is correct.
questions.hint: Check whether two different nonzero inputs can produce the same reciprocal value.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which of two cubic functions has an inverse on \(\mathbb{R}\).
questions.question: Which function has an inverse on \(\mathbb{R}\)?
questions.explanation:
For \(f(x)=x^3+2x\), the derivative is
\[
f'(x)=3x^2+2>0
\]
for all real \(x\). Thus \(f\) is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb{R}\), so it is one-to-one and has an inverse.
For \(g(x)=x^3-3x\), the derivative is
\[
g'(x)=3x^2-3=3(x-1)(x+1),
\]
which changes sign, so \(g\) is not one-to-one on \(\mathbb{R}\). Hence it does not have an inverse on \(\mathbb{R}\). Therefore, option A is correct.
questions.hint: Use monotonicity to test whether each function is one-to-one on \(\mathbb{R}\).

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether an exponential function has an inverse.
questions.question: Does \(f(x)=e^x\) have an inverse function on \(\mathbb{R}\)?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because it is strictly increasing.

questions.explanation:
The exponential function \(f(x)=e^x\) is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb{R}\). Therefore, it is one-to-one and has an inverse. Its inverse is the natural logarithm:
\[
f^{-1}(x)=\ln x.
\]
Thus option A is correct.
questions.hint: Recall whether the exponential function is increasing or decreasing on its entire domain.

questions.concept: Existence of an Inverse Function on a Restricted Domain
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether the sine function has an inverse on a restricted interval.
questions.question: Does \(f(x)=\sin x\) have an inverse function on the interval \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\)?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because it is strictly increasing on this interval.

questions.explanation: On the interval \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), the sine function is strictly increasing. Therefore, it is one-to-one on this interval and has an inverse, namely the arcsine function. Thus option A is correct.
questions.hint: Check whether the sine function is monotonic on the given restricted interval.

questions.learningObjective: Determine which function fails to have an inverse on its given domain.
questions.question: Which function does NOT have an inverse on the given domain?
questions.explanation:
The function \(f(x)=x^3\) is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb{R}\), so it is one-to-one and has an inverse.
However, \(f(x)=\sin x\) is not one-to-one on \([0,\pi]\). For example,
\[
\sin 0=0 \quad \text{and} \quad \sin \pi=0,
\]
so two different inputs give the same output. Therefore, it does not have an inverse on \([0,\pi]\). Thus option B is correct.
questions.hint: For each function, check whether two different inputs in the given domain can produce the same output.
